newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, U.S. officials to confront farm trade issues.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. officials to confront farm trade issues.

text.p: Senior U.S. and European Commission agriculture officials are set to grapple next Tuesday with farm trade disputes ranging from EU grain import tariffs and wheat subsidies to a planned veterinary agreement.
Washington will the same day urge the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Geneva to investigate EU tariffs on imports of grain, notably rice, saying they break free trade rules.
The tariff dispute "will inevitably come up (at the talks) but it's not the main issue," a European Commission spokesman said, adding that the veterinary pact would dominate discussions.
On Monday, the EU's executive said it was surprised the U.S. had taken action over tariffs at the WTO when talks were still under way.
Last week EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler proposed a tender system to help resolve a dispute with Washington over duty-free imports of U.S. rice.
An adjudication system would help solve the problem of cross-subsidisation, the Commission spokesman said.

EU rice millers have complained that U.S. exporters will use the duty-free concession to subsidise non-quota rice exports. The concession was introduced as compensation for trade losses after Austria, Sweden and Finland joined the EU.
Under the deal, U.S. traders may export an extra 38,000 tonnes of milled rice and 8,000 tonnes of brown rice duty-free.
Washington is also concerned that EU plans to introduce common veterinary import rules in the 15 member states on January 1, 1997 could severely disrupt trade.
More than $500 million of U.S. exports of meat and other veterinary products could be affected.
Any further delay of the EU move, which follows the removal of intra-EU trade barriers in January 1993, is impossible, EU officials said.
Problems remain over petfood, dairy products and eggs.
Although agreement with Washington on mutual recognition of standards is unlikely to be reached by the end-year deadline, EU officials stressed that trade would not grind to a halt.
"There will be more inspections of imports but trade will not be blocked," an official said.
Another issue worrying Washington is a recent sharp rise in EU wheat export subsidies and signs last week that Brussels was prepared to start undercutting U.S. prices.

But a senior EU grain official said after a weekly grain export tender last Thursday that the EU was still pricing its wheat against U.S. material, even though U.S. price levels scarcely reflected world markets.
Argentine wheat prices were much lower but the EU was reluctant to match them for fear of reviving a grain export subsidy war with the U.S. that raged in the early 1990s.
Another sore point is EU delay in approving imports of U.S. gene-modified maize. EU scientists are due to advise next month on whether Ciba Geigy's product is safe.

The U.S. side in the talks will be led by Paul Drazek, trade adviser to U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, and the EU team by Corrado Pirzio-Biroli, chief aide to Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler.
